subject: owl
pitch: A great horned owl perched on a gnarled branch. Mottled bark-brown and buff feathers with fine dark barring, a pale bib at the throat, tall feathered ear tufts, a round tawny facial disc rimmed in black, huge orange eyes and a hooked grey beak. Feathered legs end in strong black talons gripping the wood.
reasoning:
I'm planning out the TypeScript module structure for building an owl using the SDK, reviewing the key builder APIs for joints, chains, and paths I'll need to construct the model.

Scaling things to match a real great horned owl's proportions, around half a meter tall, and I'm thinking through how to pose it perched on a branch so the lowest point of the branch rests at y=0.

For the feet and legs, I'm thinking short feathered legs placing the feet around y~0.34, then considering whether to build the owl's torso as a simple vertical lathe shape since owls have a mostly upright posture, versus a swept path body.

Actually, I'll go with a bulbous egg-shaped lathe profile for the fat owl body, then add a loft along a slightly curved path with stations for tail, chest, and head base to get the natural forward lean, relying on a joint hierarchy (body, head) to drive the bone weighting for the sweep.

For the limbs, I'm planning wing chains with wingL1-style joints folded at the sides, leg chains with hip/knee/ankle joints for feathered legs, and digit-role toes with talons at the branch. I want to keep the script around 250-350 lines, so I'm sticking to primitives I'm confident about and sketching an import plan pulling in paint helpers like mottle, stripes, spots, and gradient for feather texturing, especially stripes with an axis parameter to create horizontal barring across the feathers.

Now I'm settling on the color palette — bark browns, buff, dark brown, pale bib, tawny facial disc, black rim, orange eyes with dark pupils, grey beak, black talons, and bark-brown branch — and figuring out how to combine a mottled base with stripe barring only on the breast region by nesting paint functions that resolve based on position and normal.

For the facial features, I'm shaping the bib as a separate pale buff-white patch, the facial disc as a flattened sphere scaled down in depth, and the dark rim as a torus positioned around the disc's edge, adjusting orientation so each piece sits correctly on the head.

I'm placing orange eyes with small black pupils onto the disc, adding backward-swept cone-shaped ear tufts in brown, and now working on the hooked beak using a swept bezier curve that tapers from a wider base down to a narrow curved tip.

Since beaks should function as openable jaws, I'm splitting it into an upper beak fixed to the head and a lower beak attached to a "jaw" joint. For the legs, I'm setting up chains running from hip to ankle to foot, working out how many named spans the path needs for the feathered tarsus and toes.

Now I'm figuring out the talons as spikes projecting forward and downward from each foot joint, three in front and one behind, using dark coloring and offset positions along the x-axis for the toe bases.

For the branch, I'm planning a gnarly catmull-spline path with a tapered, sinusoidally-varying radius for bark texture, plus a floor stub rod anchoring it, making sure the root joint ("body") sits correctly and static branch parts just attach to the nearest joint since no posing is needed there.

I'm positioning the owl's feet to rest right at the branch's top surface near x=0, adjusting leg-tip heights accordingly, and refining the branch path with five control points and a taper from thicker middle to thinner ends, plus a ground stub rod with flat caps for stability. I'm also planning small twig spikes along the branch for a gnarled look, then starting to lay out the owl's body as a loft through stations (tail, belly, chest, shoulder/neck) with specific widths and heights before moving on to building the head.

Realizing the original proportions made the owl too tall (around 0.85m vs. a real great horned owl's ~0.55m), I'm rescaling everything down—compressing the body stations to around 0.72m total height, adjusting feet at 0.345, belly, chest, and shoulder positions, and shrinking the loft widths accordingly for a more stylized but proportionate owl. I'm now beginning to define the head as a separate rounded element with its own joint position, size, and tuft height to cap off the body.

Settling on the black rim torus around the facial disc with eyes fitting inside it, then working out the hooked upper beak curve and smaller lower mandible using bezier sweeps positioned at the jaw joint. Now I'm placing the legs short and stubby with hips, ankles, and foot tips positioned to land on top of the branch.

Adding talon spikes to the toes with curled downward directions for the grip, then setting up the folded wing chains with shoulder-to-tip joint paths.

For the wing geometry itself, I'm weighing between a swept membrane and a simple flat slab polygon in the YZ plane since the wing is folded flush against the body's side.

I'll give the slab a mottled paint pattern matching the body coloring, and attach it as a static part near the shoulder rather than rigging it with joints, since the wings stay folded in this pose.

For the ear tufts, I'll sweep small spikes from base points near the top of the head outward and upward, tapering to a point, letting the nearest joint (head) handle the bone weighting automatically.

For the head itself, I'm placing a sphere geometry at the head joint, scaled slightly taller than wide, colored with the same brown mottled palette as the body rather than giving it a separate texture. I'm also sketching out how the facial disc should look -- tawny/buff coloring with a darker rim ring -- and starting to define the mottled fur color for the body paint.

Now I'm working out the plumage paint function: a pale buff bib on the throat, darker barring across the lower breast, and mottled fur elsewhere, all blended through conditional checks on position and normal direction. For the wings, I'm considering a simpler striped pattern using dark brown and tan tones along the y-axis to suggest feather barring.

Then I'm defining the other materials — feathered legs in buff-brown, dark talons, a grey beak, orange eyes with dark pupils, and a wood-grain branch texture running along the x-axis with knots and twigs.

Next I'm setting up the skeleton: a root body joint, then head, jaw, and mirrored wing joints branching off it with appropriate positions and directions, plus leg chains parented to the body, making sure each joint name and role follows the naming rules.

For the leg chains and branch mesh I'm working out how parenting and weighting work — legs rig properly to the body-rooted hip joint, while the branch sweep stays rigid to the body joint since it's unskinned, and I'm defining a tapered radius function for the branch so it narrows smoothly toward the ends with rounded caps.

I'm positioning the catmull-spline branch so the owl's feet land near its surface around y≈0.31, then adding gnarled twig spikes and a knot for texture, plus a short stub rod anchored at the ground. I'm checking that the rod's tilt doesn't let its bottom ring sink more than about 2% below the floor plane, working out the geometry of the tilted cylinder's lowest point relative to y=0.

Now I'm placing the owl's eyes: spheres for the eye discs, small dark pupil spheres protruding slightly past the disc surface, and considering whether to add a thin torus rim outline around each eye for definition.

I'm working out the beak geometry — upper and lower beak curves swept along bezier paths near the eye line — and then positioning the ear tufts as small spike bones angled outward and upward from the top of the head, checking their bases don't poke through the skull sphere.

Then I'm setting up the body loft using the station profile points weighted to a single "body" bone, confirming the head and tuft geometry stay bound to the head bone, and sketching leg and talon placement so the hip joint sits inside the body volume. Finally I'm laying out the wing as a flat slab of points along the side of the body, tapering from the shoulder down toward the tail.

Setting up the tail feather path for the owl, then double-checking paint consistency and triangle budget before finalizing the builder setup with its options and default export structure, planning imports for the painting utilities.

I'm working through the joint hierarchy next: head and jaw placement relative to their parent joints, then the leg chains with hip, ankle, and foot joints defined as polyline paths for each side.

Now I'm figuring out contact placement for talons at each foot tip, defining offsets for the forward-facing toes on each foot.

I realize the toes need to actually wrap over the branch's front surface rather than float ahead of it, so I'm recalculating the geometry to position foot tips closer to the branch center and angle the toe directions downward and forward so they visually grip the curved surface.

For the facial disc, I'll settle on a simple mottled tawny-buff color pattern instead of something more complex, then move on to double-checking the part-building function signature and its options before continuing.

For the part helper with a bone option, I'll bind explicit rigid weights to that bone. For the spike, direction input gets normalized via toDirection. For the beak I'll use a bezier curve, and catmull for the branch path, importing both from the SDK; for sweeps built from raw point arrays I'll fall back to the nearest joint at the path's start since there's no owner weighting available.

Now I'm wiring up bone assignments for the remaining parts: jaw for both beak halves, body for the tail, and chain-based sweeps for the legs. I'm placing wing joints with parent, position, and direction, adding small spike twigs branching off the main branch with their own base points and directions, and sketching a knot detail nearby. I'm also setting up paint variants -- a mottled grain for the bark, a striped cross pattern for the wing, and a darker fur-based plumage treatment for the tail.

Then I'm starting to lay out the actual owl builder code: importing the builder utilities, defining metadata, setting base colors, and constructing paint functions that combine mottling and striping -- one for the fur, one for barred feather sections, and one that picks between a pale bib color, the barred pattern, or the base fur depending on position and surface normal, to carve out the distinct bib region on the chest.

Now I'm defining the skeletal joints for the owl -- body, head, jaw, and two wings -- each anchored at specific coordinates with directional vectors to establish the pose and hierarchy before moving on to building the body loft geometry.

Still writing body loft geometry...

Now I'm placing the head sphere geometry positioned at the head joint's coordinates, checking scale options and confirming the bone binding is correct.

Adding the facial disc and eye details...

Setting the jaw joint position, then adding ear tufts as spikes with sizing adjusted so the overall silhouette stays proportional. Now I'm working on wing geometry with a striped paint pattern and slab shapes positioned outside the body surface.

Adjusting the x offset so the wing slab actually touches the chest, then defining point arrays that sweep from shoulder down to the wingtip, letting the triangulation handle orientation regardless of point order. Checking that the bone weighting and paint frame work correctly for these surfaces, then starting on the tail using a sweep along a catmull-rom curve that tapers from the body toward the tip.

Verifying the tail's radius function returns a properly typed tuple and confirming the tail hangs freely in the air behind the branch, which is visually fine. Now starting the leg chains for both sides, defining joint positions from hip down to foot...

Still writing talon spikes...

I'm removing an unused variable and double-checking the branch sweep uses a catmull curve with bark grain coloring, rigidly bound to the body bone with a radius that tapers toward both ends. I need to make sure the branch's lowest point still keeps the whole model's minimum y at zero.

Now I'm adding a stub rod to support the branch, verifying its radius contains the branch's base radius, then placing two small twig spikes with slightly tapered radii near the branch to add detail without poking through the surface.

I'm double-checking that every variable name used (fur, bars, plumage, disc, wingPaint, bark, TALON constants, seg) is actually defined, and confirming the paint helpers like mottle, stripes, and grain all use valid option signatures. I'll also verify the owl's lowest point touches the ground stub and finalize the structure, then write out the final code block.
